text.p: Insurance liberalisation in Asia will force reinsurers to re-evaluate their services to the primary insurance market or fail the test of differentiation, a senior reinsurer says.

Ben Ho, managing director of Scor Asia-Pacific, a unit of Paris-based reinsurer Scor SA, said the abolition of tariff markets would create unfamiliar territory for primary insurers and fuel a need for a range of consulting services.

"They (primary insurers) will look for more from their reinsurers. They will look for support and advice on rating, technical services, risk management and even the marketing approach," Ho told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.
He said an abundance of high security reinsurance capacity would simply not be enough to win and retain business in a fiercely competitive market.
"How do you differentiate yourself just on capacity? The capacity of SCOR is no different than the capacity of any other reinsurer," he said.

Although expansion in Asia makes for good headlines and is identified by many Western reinsurers as the key future market, Ho was doubtful that all those clamouring for a foothold would be successful.
"If you were not in early, you may already be too late," he said. "If you're a new player you may have to force price competition or take the most difficult business. Either way it can be expensive."

Scor, which has been in Asia since 1972, adopted a new structure from January 1 1996, making its Singapore $70 million capitalised unit, Scor Asia-Pacific, a regional headquarters co-ordinating operations in Hong Kong, Australia and Tokyo.

Asian operations generated gross premium income of S$111 million in 1995, or 8.0 percent of group totals, a figure which Ho said he was confident would grow substantially over the next three to five years.

"We do have ambitious plans," said Ho, who sees double-digit growth for premiums between now and the turn of the century, without changing the focus of the company's existing portfolio, which is primarily property-based.
He said Scor was actively researching new sources of income, including tapping into the rich seam of captive premium -- where companies set up their own insurance unit to save on cost.

There is a general expectation among insurers that captives will become popular risk transfer vehicles for the growing numbers of global industrial conglomerates based in Asia, as they already are in Australia and, to some degree, in Japan.
As much of the premium of captives finds its way back to the reinsurance industry, there are clear opportunities, said Ho.
"As the experience builds up and the know-how is recognised, I think Asians will be looking into it. We're at the very beginning here," Ho said.
